The CDC’s “severe seasonal flu” lean matters because it is the highest-quality source in the packet, but it is explicitly hedged. I should not convert a hedged scientific judgment into complacent policy. Severe seasonal flu is not trivial; it can still stress hospitals, and a novel virus has population-wide susceptibility, uncertain seasonality, and no vaccine. The economic advisor is right that shutdowns have real public-health consequences too: unemployment, deferred medical care, business failures, social disruption, and loss of trust if we impose dramatic measures and then appear to have overreacted. The health hawk is right about exponential growth: if this is substantially worse than flu, waiting until hospitals are full is too late. So the correct posture is not panic, but rapid preparedness under uncertainty.

I want to avoid two early mistakes. First, I do not want to downplay severity to protect markets; that buys maybe a few calm news cycles but destroys credibility if the virus accelerates. Second, I do not want to impose a national lockdown before we have enough evidence to justify it. A lockdown is a blunt instrument. If we use it too early without clear thresholds, compliance will decay precisely when we may later need it most. Instead, I want to build the capacity that will let us make sharper decisions in one or two weeks: testing, hospital surveillance, supply chains, and honest public communication.

The WHO and international reports suggest rising clusters. That is enough to increase watchfulness, especially around travel and imported cases, but because we already have domestic clusters, travel restrictions would be at best a delay tactic. They also carry diplomatic and economic costs and can create a false sense that the threat is “over there.” I’m not ruling them out, but I need better intelligence on where the affected regions are, whether travel seeding is still material relative to community spread, and whether screening/quarantine would do more than broad bans.

The social media picture is dangerous in a different way. Fake mortality memos, “just flu” narratives, and rumors of bodies in the streets can each cause harm. If government communication is vague or political, the information space will be filled by speculation. So I want daily candid briefings: not performative alarm, not reassurance theater, but clear uncertainty bands, what we know, what we don’t, and what would trigger stronger action. This also lets us tell people practical steps: stay home when sick, protect nursing homes and hospitals, improve hygiene, local authorities should prepare distancing plans, and clinicians should report unusual pneumonia clusters.

The highest-value early actions are low-regret investments. Testing and surveillance are urgent because the most dangerous thing right now is blindness. Hospital data are equally important: test positivity can be biased by who gets tested, but ER visits, ICU admissions, ventilator use, and pneumonia deaths can reveal whether severe disease is rising. CDC needs to refine clinical guidance and case definitions, but I do not want CDC alone grading its own homework; I want testing systems, hospitals, and international reporting queried in parallel. Social intelligence also matters, not because rumors are true, but because rumors can signal local anomalies or misinformation campaigns that require response.

I also think we should begin industrial preparedness now. Invoking the Defense Production Act for PPE, tests, and ventilators is not the same as locking down the country. It is insurance. If this fizzles, we have replenished strategic capacity. If it grows, the time lost in manufacturing cannot be recovered. I would rather be accused of buying too many masks and swabs than explain why nurses are reusing equipment because we waited for perfect fatality estimates.

Similarly, a crash vaccine and therapeutics program is a long lead-time bet. It will not solve Week 1 transmission, but it is exactly the kind of federal action that must start before the need is obvious. The cost is real, but small compared with the potential cost of a prolonged epidemic. Even if several candidates fail, platform development, trials infrastructure, and antiviral screening have national-security value.

On economic relief, I would not yet push emergency household payments if we are not asking people to stop working nationally. But I do want Congress engaged now. If local closures become necessary, relief must arrive with the order, not months later. I also want statutory authorities and funding ready for testing, state health departments, hospital surge, paid sick leave, and small-business support if conditions worsen.

So my Week 1 course: do not lock down nationally, do not downplay, do not simply defer. Lead federally by gathering facts fast, preparing supplies, launching biomedical countermeasures, and speaking honestly. I’ll ask governors to prepare local mitigation plans and protect high-risk settings, but the federal government should set the tempo on surveillance, procurement, and public truth-telling.
